1.pericope_label: Hezekiah rends his clothes: the children come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth

schools.summary: Fill in the setting from the penitential custom and the invader's own inscriptions, take the coming of God at its widest, and prefer a spirit put into the man over a physical blast.

Read the errand as a request for consolation out of doctrine rather than for shared lamentation, defend a king who sought fresh confirmations as no distruster, and take the blast for a whirlwind driving chaff.
Name Persian dualism and the manuscript evidence, and identify the blast with the pestilential wind the Arabs call simoom, which is the angel that later smites the camp.
Read the whole assault as an attack that misfires, driving the king toward God rather than away, and turn every step of it into a rule about prayer.

debates.question: What is the blast that God promises to send upon him?

positions.view: a pestilential wind of the kind the Arabs call simoom, identified outright with the angel who later smites the camp, against Secker's ruling that the phrase can only mean putting a spirit into a person
a spirit put into him, an impulse strong enough to overpower previous resolves, the received rendering wrongly suggesting the later physical calamity
neither the divine Spirit nor the plague but a whirlwind, wicked men being driven like chaff wherever God pleases
a pestilential blast, such as afterwards destroyed the army
the return and the second attempt on the city, without comment on the means

debates.question: Does the perhaps of the fourth verse admit real doubt?

positions.view: no; believers speak so when perplexed by a case though certain of the outcome, as an apostle's if perhaps this thought may be forgiven thee was meant to strike the mind
not questioning but hoping and encouraging himself
it is an encouragement to pray though we have but some hope of mercy, and should make us ply the oar of prayer with double diligence

debates.question: Why did the king send messengers rather than go himself?

positions.view: because he was at prayer in the temple, while the prophet stayed at home not for ease but so that the king's faith might be tried by his absence
the reason cannot be said, and two versions read that the prophet was sent, which does not agree with the Hebrew
the errand's point is that at last the people saw their teacher, the prophet they had derided being their one resource

outliers.reading: Alone reads the whole assault as an attack that misfires, the taunt frightening the king toward God rather than away from him, as a wind that fails to strip a traveller's coat only makes him wrap it closer.

Alone names an opponent by name, refusing Archbishop Secker's ruling that the phrase can only mean putting a spirit into a person, and alone dates Persian dualism early enough to be the target of the declaration about light and darkness.

themes: And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah heard it, that he rent his clothes, and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the Lord.
And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, unto Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz.
And they said unto him, Thus saith Hezekiah, This day is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of blasphemy: for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth.

It may be the Lord thy God will hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of Assyria his master hath sent to reproach the living God, and will reprove the words which the Lord thy God hath heard: wherefore lift up thy prayer for the remnant that is left.
So the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah.
And Isaiah said unto them, Thus shall ye say unto your master, Thus saith the Lord, Be not afraid of the words that thou hast heard, wherewith the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.
Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.

8.pericope_label: The letter of Sennacherib: where are the gods of Hamath, of Arphad, and of Sepharvaim

schools.summary: Place the towns from the old allotment and stop honestly where the topography fails, identify the Ethiopian from the Assyrian inscriptions, and supply the geography of the conquered places from the annals.
Argue from the letters themselves that the army stayed before the city, and treat the blasphemy as the point: to call the author of truth a deceiver takes from God what is most absolutely his own.
Reconstruct the movements as a siege raised under pressure, emend the repeated verb to he returned, and find a modern parallel for the manifesto in a proclamation issued to the Parisians in 1792.
Note that no reply was sent because God had taken the work in hand, and that it is bad to talk proudly and profanely but worse to write so.

debates.question: Where had the invader moved, and why?

positions.view: the first siege was raised under pressure and a second town taken up as the easier conquest
both towns belong to the old allotment of Judah and the move looks strategic, meant to intercept the Ethiopian advance, though in our ignorance of the ground nothing further can be settled
toward Egypt, a camp moved to meet the coming armies early
the army stayed before the city while the spokesman went back alone, since the letters presuppose a siege still in place

debates.question: How did the Assyrian know what had been promised to the city?

positions.view: no leak by a traitor need be supposed, since the promises were common talk and the people gloried in them openly
the message repeats its predecessors, made more defiant by the threat from Tirhakah
the letter grants the title king of Judah, which the servant had refused

debates.question: What weight should be given to the written form of the threat?

positions.view: it is worse to write proudly and profanely than to speak so, since writing argues deliberation, spreads further and lasts longer
the sheets are one letter, not two
the repeated verb of the ninth verse is a copyist's echo, the true reading being he returned, which yields the idiom he sent again

outliers.reading: Alone reaches for a modern parallel to the manifesto, a proclamation issued to the Parisians in 1792 that he calls the forerunner of a torrent of blood, whose author met a ruin he thinks nearly like this one.

Alone anatomises the boast about ancestral conquests, observing that tyrants glory in ancestral crimes without asking whether the conquests were just, so that the mightiest monarch is often best called the rich son of a great robber.

themes: So Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish.
And he heard say concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, He is come forth to make war with thee. And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,
Thus shall ye speak to Hezekiah king of Judah, saying, Let not thy God, in whom thou trustest, deceive thee, saying, Jerusalem shall not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.
Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands by destroying them utterly; and shalt thou be delivered?
Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed, as Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which were in Telassar?
Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arphad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?

14.pericope_label: Spread before the LORD: thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth

schools.summary: Read the spreading of the letter as a legal act, the evidence laid before the judge, and supply an Assyrian parallel for it; bound the concession precisely, admitting the facts and denying only the inference.

Deny that the letter informs God, since the act is an accommodation that inflames the suppliant, take the titles as arguments, and hold the cherubim to the form of the ark against the reading that makes them angels.
Prefer the plural throughout, put the prayer in the sanctuary, and restore the words the received text has lost.

debates.question: Why was the letter spread out before the LORD?

positions.view: as a mute appeal to the supreme arbiter, the evidence laid before the judge before a word is spoken
not because God needs informing, since he knows our wants before we ask, but in accommodation to our weakness, and because the act inflames the suppliant
because the king returned no railing and wrote no reply, leaving the letter to be answered by the one it insulted
the prayer is in the sanctuary, and the plural should be kept throughout

debates.question: What is meant by dwelling between the cherubim?

positions.view: the form of the ark, where the promise of presence attached, and not the angels among whom God might be said to reign in heaven
the glory-cloud between the ark's figures, which themselves stand for the elemental powers of the sky, the same expression elsewhere describing storm clouds
the mercy seat and the presence that rested there, one of three titles each carrying its own argument for faith

debates.question: How far does the concession about the burnt gods go?

positions.view: the facts are admitted and the inference alone denied, since those gods went to the fire or to Nineveh as trophies, but one who has no graven image cannot
the distinction between true and false gods is the beginning of piety, against men who rest in dark speculation and touch neither heaven nor earth
the received word for lands destroys the sense, fifteen manuscripts and the parallel giving nations instead
the prayer ends here and the reply begins

outliers.reading: Alone supplies an Assyrian parallel for the gesture, a king who on receiving a defiant message from Elam went into his goddess's temple, reminded her what he had done for her, and got his answer as a night vision.

Alone turns the cherubim into a rule about nearness, that the divine majesty cannot be confined to our understanding yet comes down in word and sign so feeble minds may climb by degrees, the sacraments serving as ladders that superstition turns the other way.

themes: And Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up unto the house of the Lord, and spread it before the Lord.
And Hezekiah prayed unto the Lord, saying,
O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, that dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth: thou hast made heaven and earth.
Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear; open thine eyes, O Lord, and see: and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent to reproach the living God.
Of a truth, Lord, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations, and their countries,
And have cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods, but the work of men’s hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them.
Now therefore, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the Lord, even thou only.

21.pericope_label: The virgin daughter of Zion hath despised thee: whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed

schools.summary: Date the reply as the prophet's last recorded utterance, set the taunt beside the same title used of Zidon, and show from the royal inscriptions how conventional the boasts about mountains and water were.
Hear the address to the whole church as heightening the baseness of the scorn, treat the reproach as offered to God himself, and keep the water threat local to the besieged city.
Restore the lost verb of hearing, correct servants to messengers and the height of his border to his retreat, and set a Latin poet's Alaric beside the boast about drying rivers.
Note that the answer came in writing because too long for word of mouth, and that the enemy may bark but cannot bite.

debates.question: What are the rivers the invader threatens to dry up?

positions.view: the canals of Egypt, the word for that country also carrying the sense of fortified enclosure, so that the sentence defies the Ethiopian and not Jerusalem
the canals and artificial lakes that ringed the Egyptian cities
the city's own water, some finding the spring and cisterns here, the threat being to leave it dry enough to kill by thirst
the perfects here stand out against the surrounding futures as statements of what actually happened

debates.question: How is the boast about climbing the mountains to be taken?

positions.view: as a convention of Assyrian royal inscriptions, two kings boasting of trackless paths and rugged mountains unsuited to chariots, so that the phrase may have become a proverb for surmounting obstacles
as relating to the present siege rather than to former victories generally, the invader treating the country as already his
as needing correction, the height of his border being properly his lodge or retreat

debates.question: What does the taunt in the mouth of the virgin daughter accomplish?

positions.view: it reverses an earlier oracle in which the virgin was ravished by invaders, this one escaping the ravisher and laughing his lust to scorn
it carries more force addressed to the whole church than to the king, the city being an orphan insulted by a ruffian
it shows that those who magnify themselves against God's people vilify themselves, the enemy barking but unable to bite
it is the sentence the LORD has pronounced in answer to the prayer

outliers.reading: Alone dates the reply chronologically, calling the prophecy that follows this prophet's last recorded utterance and inviting attention to its contacts with his earlier work and with the long poem traditionally ascribed to him.
Alone sets a Latin poet's Alaric beside the boast about drying rivers, who saw mountains sink under his feet and rivers dry, broke the Alps and ladled the Po with victorious helmets.

themes: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent unto Hezekiah, saying, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Whereas thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria:
This is the word which the Lord hath spoken concerning him; The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee.
Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? even against the Holy One of Israel.

By thy servants hast thou reproached the Lord, and hast said, By the multitude of my chariots am I come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon; and I will cut down the tall cedars thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the height of his border, and the forest of his Carmel.
I have digged, and drunk water; and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of the besieged places.

26.pericope_label: Hast thou not heard long ago: I will put my hook in thy nose and turn thee back

schools.summary: Take the thing done long ago as the invader's own career, planned and foreseen so that his conquests were a counsel he unwittingly served, and correct the text of the weakness images.

Refuse the majority reading and make the thing made long ago the city itself, so that the verse asks whether God will now ruin what he founded, and press the housetop grass against the prosperity of the wicked.
Cut through two words that have embarrassed every interpreter, prefer blasted to parched on the manuscripts, and gather the eastern evidence for the ring in the nose.

debates.question: What was done and formed long ago?

positions.view: the invader's whole career, planned and foreseen, his conquests a counsel he unwittingly served rather than his own power
the city itself, named by a pronoun only, the verse being a question — shall I now bring this to ruin as I brought the rest?
the report of ancient times, heard by the invader from the histories or from the prophets
the laying waste of warlike nations, once the received pair of words is corrected on the Greek

debates.question: What is made of the grass upon the housetops?

positions.view: the higher it grows the nearer the heat and the sooner it withers, no passer-by blesses it, and corn at our feet outvalues herbage on a roof
one emblem of frailty following another, with an error of transcription betrayed by the italics of the last clause
the word rendered parched has no authority and should be blasted, on six manuscripts
the conquered were short of hand because their strength had been taken away beforehand, which spoils the conqueror's boast
Asshur is the chosen instrument against nations too short-handed to resist him, until the lion is placed under restraint

debates.question: Is the metal put in the nose a hook or a ring?

positions.view: a ring, since hooks are for catching fish and would not suit a beast
a ring, on the Aramaic version and Jerome, the iron one put through a camel's nostrils, which the Talmud allows her to wear on the sabbath
whatever the metal, the Assyrian sculptures show beasts and men alike dragged in this way

outliers.reading: Alone turns the founding of the city into a survey of empires, asking where the majesty of Rome has gone and calling what survives of the world's mistress a workshop of iniquity, while the church, small and feeble, is renewed age by age through resurrections.

themes: Hast thou not heard long ago, how I have done it; and of ancient times, that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste defenced cities into ruinous heaps.

Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded: they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up.
But I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me.
Because thy rage against me, and thy tumult, is come up into mine ears, therefore will I put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest.

30.pericope_label: A sign in three years: the remnant taking root downward and bearing fruit upward

schools.summary: Date the sign to the autumn near the equinox, insist that it is only a sign if the second year is still future, and spell out the two siege operations that are denied.
Answer the objection that a sign should not follow the event by distinguishing two kinds of sign, and press the promise of increase against a remnant so small the ground looked uprooted.

debates.question: Which years does the sign of the self-sown harvest cover?

positions.view: the current year, in which the enemy had kept the people from their fields, since on the alternative reckoning nothing would be signified at all
the year about to open at the autumn equinox, tillage having stopped in spring, with the land clear only twelve months later
the years of scarcity after the wasting of the fields, in which food is promised without sowing until the third
the sign is given to the king and not to the invader, the word carrying the sense of a wonder

debates.question: Can a sign properly follow the event it confirms?

positions.view: yes; signs are of two kinds, some going before to lead us by the hand and others following to fix the event deeply, as a people brought out of Egypt were told beforehand they would sacrifice three days after
the sign lies within the nearer future and pledges a prediction of wider range

debates.question: What is denied to the besieger?

positions.view: not merely the capture of the city but the usual operations of a siege, the advance under locked shields and the raising of earthworks
the last word denotes an engine that throws darts rather than a mound, since mounds are not poured
he will lose his labour and make straight home without turning aside
the prophecy of protection becomes more definite here than it has ever been before

outliers.reading: Alone reports that the definiteness of this closing section has been urged against its authorship, Hitzig calling it suspiciously precise and Knobel finding no reason to doubt the prophet wrote it.
Alone runs the word escaped forward to the elect, listing what they are not delivered from — the fall, its imputation, corrupt nature — before naming justice, the law's curse and the wrath to come.

themes: And this shall be a sign unto thee, Ye shall eat this year such as groweth of itself; and the second year that which springeth of the same: and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof.
And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward:
For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this.
Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it.
By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the Lord.

35.pericope_label: I will defend this city: the angel of the LORD, and the sons that smote him in the house of his god

schools.summary: Separate the two motives of the defence, explain the destruction as an epidemic that a prophet would call the angel, weigh the Egyptian version against the biblical record, and read the murder out of the inscriptions.
Deny that the people's merits are in view, refuse the plague explanation on the numbers, and read the shameful flight and the parricide as the ordinary end of tyrants.
Recall the prophecy of a people saved without bow or sword, and close on the blasphemer's punishment.

debates.question: How was the Assyrian camp destroyed?

positions.view: by an epidemic spreading over days and brought to a head in one night, which a prophet accustomed to see the winds as messengers called the angel of the LORD
not by plague at all; so many dying in a night cannot be pestilence, and the explanation is an invention by which Satan, through profane historians, has darkened an extraordinary judgment
by an angel sent forth from heaven, in the same night as the message to the king
as foretold, that this people would be saved not by bow or sword but by their God

debates.question: Why did the sons kill their father?

positions.view: because the ambition that reached for other men's lands could not keep peace at home, the plot growing from neglect of some sons and fondness for another
because a will left the chief treasures and a new royal title to what seems a younger son, whose elder brothers revenged themselves on the father
as an awful punishment of blasphemy, since none can harden his neck against God and prosper

debates.question: For whose sake is the city defended?

positions.view: for the assertion of a majesty that had been blasphemed and for the remembering of a promise, the good a man leaves surviving as his evil does
for God's own purpose and not for anything in the people, David being named for the promise and not the person, so that the verse gives no footing to the intercession of saints
because a shielded people cannot be hurt
the account of the catastrophe is appended to this culminating prophecy

outliers.reading: Alone brings modern parallels to the destruction, the wind that scattered the Armada and the frost that broke a march from Moscow, and alone reports the Egyptian version out of Herodotus in which field mice gnawed the invaders' bowstrings at Pelusium, preferring writers with documents to the travellers' tales the vergers of Egyptian temples told.

themes: For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.
Then the angel of the Lord went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh.

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esar–haddon his son reigned in his stead.
